newsitem.title: USA: UFO cult leader once lived ordinary life.
newsitem.headline: UFO cult leader once lived ordinary life.

text.p: The man who led 38 followers in a shocking mass suicias a preacher's son and devoted himself to music before joining up with a nurse to establish what became one of America's most bizarre cults.

The 66-year-old Marshall Applewhite, known to his followers as "Do" (pronounced Doe), was the son of a Presbyterian minister who once hoped to preach himself. Instead he gravitated toward music and worked as a choral director in the early 1960s at the University of Alabama.

Colleagues from the school recall him as an offbeat character who went by his middle name, Herff, dressed casually at a time when even the students wore coats and ties and directed the school's chorus in its first-ever pop music performance. But they said he never seemed overtly strange or in any way dangerous.

All that changed in the early 1970s, when Applewhite, then living in Texas, was hospitalized with heart trouble and almost died. While recovering he met a nurse, Bonnie Lu Trusdale Nettles, who became his spiritual companion and co-founder of a group built on beliefs in asceticism, aliens and the Apocalypse.

"There was never a coming together in that we were bed partners," Applewhite later recalled in a 1992 videotape for followers. "But there was something that compelled us to spend time together and listen to each other and search together."

He said the two initially concentrated on the Scriptures and New Age material, but later decided to develop their own faith called "The Process". Applewhite and Nettles cast themselves as heavenly messengers from outer space, and in a prophecy mirroring the Christian ressurection tradition, said they would be murdered and ascend into the clouds.

Applewhite left his wife and two children to live a nomadic life with Nettles and recruited followers to join them on the UFO ride to a better life. In 1974 they persuaded several residents of a coastal town in Oregon to go with them to Colorado, where a spaceship would pick them up.

Followers were told to give away all their possessions, including their children, as well as all physical pleasures like alcohol, sex and drugs. Applewhite and Nettles, who by this point were going by the names "Bo" and "Peep", also instructed members to assume new names, which ranged from the Biblicly inspired Peter, Josua and Judas, to less traditional names such as "Window" and "Moneybags".

After one couple apparently left their two young children to followe Bo and Peep, the group attracted the attention of the police. That notoriety spread when a 1975 "liftoff" to space failed to occur and some followers became disillusioned.

A New York Times article on the cult in 1976 said one ex-member filed a complaint saying she had been defrauded after paying for a space trip. The couple were also jailed briefly after they were found to be in possession of stolen credit cards, which they said had been given to them by their followers.

After the run-ins with the law they continued their mission underground, advising followers that Oregon, Colorado and Arizona, were "high energy places." But Applewhite later remarked on the large number of "advanced souls" living in southern California.

Critics frequently dismissed Applewhite as a con artist in a moneymaking scheme. But no large amounts of money from followers were ever traced to him, and people who knew him said he seemed to have strong psychic powers and the ability to brainwash people.

In the early 1990s, after Nettles died and wtih Applewhite keeping a low profile, the group resurfaced around Chicago where members handed out fliers declaring "We're back." In 1993 the group ran a full-page advertisement in USA Today proclaiming "UFO Cult Resurfaces with Final Offer," and Applewhite again began going public with his preachings.
"I'm so happy, because my time is short here," he told followers in a videotape. "If you come with us, your time here can be shortened."
